picks.why: The definitive account of Madeira's famous irrigation channels, from workers dangling in baskets off cliffs to five centuries of water law, the walking paths and forests, all told with first-hand local knowledge.
A spirited, critical inquiry into when and how Madeira was really discovered, weighing legends and chroniclers before concluding the islands were known before Zarco's 'official' landing.
A dramatic narrative of the 1566 Huguenot corsair raid that plundered Funchal for sixteen days, driven by a renegade's revenge and followed by diplomatic fallout.
An impassioned, polemical history of how the primeval forest that gave Madeira its name was burned, felled and exported, and a plea to save what remained.
The story of Madeira wine from Cadamosto's day to the 1930s: British merchant dominance, oidium and phylloxera, fraud, grape types and how the wine was made.
Explains how the capital took its name from fennel in its valley and became the first city of Portugal's overseas empire, with period descriptions of the amphitheatre city.
A clear portrait of the island's volcanic birth around Curral das Freiras, its rocks, lava tubes and fajãs, linked to local stone names and building uses.
A vivid chronicle of four centuries of Madeiran riots, from Porto Santo's false prophets and a deposed governor to stoning mobs, election shootings and the bread and milk riots of the 1930s.
Why Victorian Europe sent its consumptives to Funchal: the island's famous climate explained through doctors' testimonies, measurements and the daily cycle of cloud and breeze.
How the empty island was settled from about 1425, with great forest fires, slaves, land grants and near-sovereign captains, the founding chapter of Madeiran society.
A frank, often critical assessment of the British in Madeira, covering their designs on the island, their grip on the wine trade, their privileges and their proud aloofness.
A gripping, detailed account of German U-boats sinking ships in Funchal harbour and shelling the city in 1916 and 1917, with names of the dead and the panic that followed.
A chronicle of the flash floods that repeatedly devastated Madeira, above all the catastrophe of 1803 that killed some 600 people, a theme still painfully relevant today.
Traces the sugar cane that made Madeira rich in the 1500s and spread across the Atlantic world, then its collapse and 19th-century revival.
A lively, affectionate picture of rural pilgrimage festivals, with singing groups on the road, improvised verses, fireworks, espetadas on laurel skewers and pilgrims fulfilling vows.
The full biography of Madeira's discoverer and first captain, covering the debate over his name, his homes, family, disputed death date, sword and statue.
The hillside parish above Funchal, with its legend of the Virgin's apparition, the island's greatest pilgrimage, its quintas, railway and famous wicker toboggans.
A portrait of the remote, uninhabited Savage Islands, covering shearwater hunts, legends of buried treasure and Shackleton's plan to search for it.
The history and treasures of Funchal's Manueline cathedral, with its celebrated cedar ceiling and a chronology running from the Huguenot sack to the 1940 museum.
Covers Madeira's folk songs with their supposed Moorish echoes, the braguinha and rajão, cathedral chapel masters and the island's 19th-century musical life.
How football arrived with a sailor's ball in 1865 and grew into Marítimo's 1926 national title, alongside cricket, tennis, sailing and the first motor car.

near_misses.why: Important history of the embroidery industry and its social impact, but only three chapters.
Charming account of Napoleon's stop off Funchal en route to St Helena, but short.
Dramatic story of the Scottish missionary-doctor and the 1846 riot, but narrow and only three chapters.
Columbus's Madeiran connections are a popular topic, but the article dwells heavily on a demolished house.
The romantic Machim legend is delightful, but it overlaps with the discovery article and is short.
Substantial social history of mental asylums, though less appealing to a general reader.
A moving tale of villagers building their own Gothic church, but a minor parish.
Gripping account of the 1856 epidemic, but only three chapters, and the disaster theme is already covered by the floods article.
Rich wine folklore and vintage customs, but it would largely duplicate the wine industry article.
Colourful account of the 1922 centenary festivities, but of narrower interest.
Attractive parish entry on seals, fishermen and wine, but parish entries tend to be formulaic.
